ancestors.notes: Direct descent from Old/Medieval Castilian (Toledo norm), itself from Hispanic Vulgar Latin.
Basque/Aquitanian substrate in the Castilian homeland: the Latin f->h change (filium>hijo), reinforcement of the 5-vowel system.
Visigothic (Gothic) superstrate: lexical layer (guerra, guardar, ropa, ganso) and some onomastics.
Andalusi Arabic adstrate: ~4000 loanwords (alcohol, almohada, aceite), inherited via the medieval stage.

name: Castilian Spanish
notes: Standard Peninsular Castilian Spanish (español castellano) per the Real Academia Española (RAE) and Asociación de Academias de la Lengua Española. Spoken natively by ~47 million in Spain; ~500 million worldwide as a first or second language. KEY FEATURES of Standard Castilian (distinción variety): (1) DISTINCIÓN: /θ/ ≠ /s/ — ⟨c⟩ before e/i and ⟨z⟩ = /θ/ (interdental fricative); absent in Latin American Spanish and in Andalusian/Canarian (seseo). (2) APICO-ALVEOLAR /s/ [s̺]: the standard Castilian s is produced with the tongue tip (apex) touching the upper alveolar ridge — a conservative feature shared with Asturian and Galician but absent from Portuguese (predorsal). (3) YEÍSMO: ⟨ll⟩ = ⟨y⟩ = /ʝ/ in modern standard (RAE 2010 norm); the historical /ʎ/ distinction is preserved in some regions (NW Spain, Río de la Plata). (4) BETACISM: ⟨b⟩ = ⟨v⟩ = /b/ (complete, unlike Portuguese). (5) VELAR FRICATIVE /x/: ⟨j⟩ and ⟨g+e,i⟩ = /x/ (or [χ] before back vowels in some varieties). (6) SILENT ⟨h⟩: etymological F- underwent F→H→∅ change: FILIU→hijo, FACERE→hacer. (7) LENITION: voiced stops /b, d, ɡ/ → spirants [β, ð, ɣ] everywhere except after a pause and after a nasal, and /d/ also after /l/; the rule holds across a word boundary (Navarro Tomás 1918, § 82 p. 63, § 101 p. 75, § 129 p. 109): cabra [ˈkaβɾa], barba [ˈbaɾβa], algo [ˈalɣo], verde [ˈbeɾðe], la boca [la ˈβoka], against hombre, caldo, un día, el domingo. (8) Word-final /d/ → [ð] or [∅]: verdad [berˈdað]/[berˈda]. (9) DIPHTHONGS ARE ASYMMETRIC: a rising diphthong has a consonantal onglide ([j w] — nación [naˈθjon], cuando [ˈkwando]) while a falling diphthong has a non-syllabic VOWEL offglide ([i̯ u̯] — aire [ˈai̯ɾe], causa [ˈkau̯sa]), per Hualde (2005 ch. 4) and RAE/ASALE NGLE Fonética y fonología (2011 ch. 8). The written accent marks stress, not hiatus: a tilde on the OPEN vowel leaves the rising diphthong intact (⟨ió⟩ in nación, ⟨iá⟩ in Adrián, ⟨ué⟩ in después), and only a tilde on the HIGH vowel signals hiatus (día, búho, continúo) — which is why ⟨iá ié ió uá ué uó⟩ are graphemes here and ⟨ía íe úa …⟩ deliberately are not. (10) VIBRANTE MÚLTIPLE: the /r/–/ɾ/ contrast is intervocalic only; in onset after a heterosyllabic /l n s/ only the trill occurs (alrededor, honra, Israel). (11) NASAL ASSIMILATION: a coda nasal is bilabial [m] before a labial (inmaculada [immakuˈlaða]). (12) WORD-INITIAL ⟨hie-, hia-, hio-⟩: the etymological silent ⟨h⟩ leaves a prevocalic high front vocoid in absolute word-initial position, where Spanish strengthens it to the palatal obstruent /ʝ/ rather than the glide [j]: hielo [ˈʝelo], hierba [ˈʝeɾba], hierro [ˈʝero], hiato [ˈʝato]. The orthography itself records this: the RAE admits the doublets yerba/hierba, yedra/hiedra and yero/hiero, i.e. the same word spelt with ⟨ye-⟩, which can only be /ʝe/. The strengthening is positional, not lexical — after a vowel the vocoid stays a glide (antihielo [antiˈjelo], contrahierba [kontɾaˈjeɾba]), which is why these are word-initial positional graphemes and not plain graphemes (Hualde 2005; Navarro Tomás 1977; RAE/ASALE NGLE Fonética y fonología 2011). (13) ⟨tx⟩ = /tʃ/: an unassimilated Basque graphotactic sequence that Spanish keeps in Basque-origin lexis and proper names — pintxo, txakolí, txapela, Arantxa, Getxo, Etxebarria. ⟨tx⟩ is not a native Spanish sequence, so no Spanish word is affected; without the entry ⟨x⟩ takes its own /ks/ value and yields the impossible *[ˈpintkso]. The value is Basque ⟨tx⟩ = /tʃ/ (Hualde & Ortiz de Urbina 2003), confirmed from the Spanish side by the RAE hispanicisation chapela ← Basque txapela, which renders the same sequence as ⟨ch⟩. (14) ⟨ý⟩: not modern RAE orthography, but it occurs in Spanish toponyms and surnames (Aýna, Ýñiguez) and in transliterated names (Almatý). It is listed with the vocalic value of ⟨y⟩ purely so the letter is not dropped; it makes no claim about accentuation and is deliberately absent from marked_vowels. Sources: Quilis (1999), Penny (2002), Hualde (2014).

sources.author: Navarro Tomás, T.
sources.title: Manual de pronunciación española
sources.notes: First edition, read in the archive.org scan. § 47: written y in the diphthongs ay, ey, oy is the semivowel [i̯]. § 122: y in syllable onset is the palatal fricative (cayado, ayer, bueyes, hoyo, ayuda). §§ 82, 101-102, 128-129: b, d, g are stops only after a pause and after a nasal (d also after l), and fricatives everywhere else, across words too. § 156: an unaccented word of two or more syllables that ends in a consonant other than n or s is oxytone (vivac, querub). § 87: a word-final n before a word-initial p or b is [m] (un buen baile, en pie, sin par). § 133: a syllable-final n before a velar is the velar nasal [ŋ], inside a word (cinco, banco, monja) and across words (en casa, sin gana). §§ 111, 149 give the same [ŋ] in cinco, nunca and lonja.

stress.notes: RAE accentuation rules: written accent wins (á é í ó ú). Default paroxytone for words ending in a vowel, -n, or -s. Words ending in any other consonant (r, l, d, z, j, x, k, f, t, c, b, p, g, m, and consonant clusters) are oxytone. Navarro Tomás 1918, § 156 p. 140: «Se pronuncia aguda, con acento sobre la última sílaba, toda palabra de dos o más sílabas escrita sin acento y terminada en cualquier consonante que no sea n ni s», with vivac and querub among its examples. The final_stress_endings list encodes the oxytone-attracting consonant endings; penult_stress_endings encodes -n/-s/-ns as explicit paroxytone attractors (overriding the default for coda -n/-s when stress position is ambiguous). Proparoxytones (esdrújulas) always carry a written accent so marked_vowels captures them. CLITICS: cliticless_words lists the Spanish prosodic clitics (palabras atonas) — definite articles, atonic indefinite article, al/del contractions, monosyllabic prepositions plus para, the atonic conjunctions y/e/o/u/ni/que and conditional si, the weak object pronouns me/te/se/le/les/nos/os and the prenominal possessives mi/tu/su(+plurals) — which lean on their host and carry no word stress (Navarro Tomas 1977, Manual de pronunciacion espanola, palabras inacentuadas; Hualde 2005, The Sounds of Spanish, prosody; RAE-ASALE Nueva gramatica, prosodia). Tonic homographs written with an accent (si 'yes', el 'he', mi/tu 'me/you', se 'I know') and the negation 'no' are excluded. Final -y after a vowel: the letter writes the off-glide of a falling diphthong, 'en los diptongos ai, ei, oi, que a veces se escriben en la forma ay, ey, oy, la i (y) se pronuncia ... más corta' (ley [ˈlei̯], buey, soy; Navarro Tomás 1918, Manual de pronunciación española, § 47, p. 39), and § 50, p. 41 repeats that the written y of ley, rey, doy, soy 'se pronuncia como i'. For accentuation such a word counts as consonant-final: oxytones ending in -y take no tilde (guirigay, virrey, convoy, estoy) and paroxytones ending in -y do (yérsey, yóquey) (RAE-ASALE, Diccionario panhispánico de dudas, 2nd ed., s.v. tilde, § 1.2.1-1.2.2). The endings ay, ey, oy, uy encode that rule. A consonant+y ending is not a Spanish spelling: rugby and sexy are unadapted English forms whose adaptations are rugbi and sexi (DPD s.v. rugbi, sexi), so they keep the default paroxytone. DIPHTHONGS: the list holds the orthographic diphthongs and triphthongs of the RAE/ASALE Ortografía (2010), as the JMIM summary of its changes quotes them (rae_ortografia_2010_nueva.pdf, p. JMIM-8): 'se consideran siempre diptongos a efectos ortográficos las combinaciones de vocal abierta (/a/, /e/, /o/) seguida o precedida de vocal cerrada átona (/i/, /u/): diario, pie…, y de dos vocales cerradas distintas (/i/, /u/): huir, muy…' (Ort. 2010, p. 235), and 'buey, fiais, lieis… son monosílabas a efectos ortográficos' (Ort. 2010, p. 237). Every other vowel sequence is a hiatus: two equal vowels (Rociito, leer), two open vowels (tea-tro, p. JMIM-16), and an open vowel next to a stressed closed one, which always takes the accent: 'país, había, reír, oír, Raúl, fíe, río, dúo, prohíben, vehículo' (Ort. 1999, p. 46, quoted on p. JMIM-8). A silent ⟨h⟩ does not divide the vowels: 'Las palabras que tienen h muda intercalada se separan como si dicha letra no existiera: al- / cohol, no *alco- /hol; prohi- / bir, no *pro- / hibir' (p. JMIM-16). ⟨ü⟩ is the closed vowel /u/ of güe, güi. Word-final ⟨y⟩ is not listed, because the syllabifier reads ⟨y⟩ by its role.

allophone_rules.notes: Vibrante múltiple after a heterosyllabic coronal (Navarro Tomás 1977; Hualde 2005 ch. 9 'Rhotics'; RAE/ASALE NGLE Fonética y fonología 2011 ch. 6; Quilis 1993). The /r/–/ɾ/ contrast is a strictly INTERVOCALIC one (caro ~ carro); everywhere else the distribution is predictable. In syllable onset after a heterosyllabic /l n s/ only the trill occurs — alrededor [alreðeˈðoɾ], honra [ˈonra], Israel [israˈel] — because Spanish has no tautosyllabic /lr nr sr/ onsets, so the rhotic in those strings always begins its own syllable and is always [r]. This is why the rule can be stated on the PRECEDING phoneme alone and needs no syllabification: the obstruent+liquid onsets that do exist (/pɾ bɾ tɾ dɾ kɾ ɡɾ fɾ/ — padre, tres, abrir) never have /l n s/ as their first element and are untouched.

Asimilación de las nasales — a coda nasal takes the point of articulation of the following consonant (Navarro Tomás 1977; Hualde 2005 ch. 3; Quilis 1993; RAE/ASALE NGLE Fonética y fonología 2011). Before a labial the surface nasal is bilabial [m], whatever the spelling: inmaculada [immakuˈlaða], envase [emˈbase], ONPE [ˈompe], un peso [um ˈpeso]. This rule asserts the LABIAL branch. ES_NASAL_VELAR asserts the velar branch, and the dental/palatal branches are sub-phonemic diacritic detail ([n̪] ante /t d/, [ɲ] ante /tʃ/) that every gold set in the board strips.

A syllable-final nasal inside a word is velar before a velar consonant. Navarro Tomás (1918, § 133, pp. 111-112): «La n final de sílaba, en contacto con una consonante velar siguiente, se asimila en la conversación ordinaria, por lo que a la posición de la lengua se refiere, a la articulación de dicha consonante velar». His examples inside a word are cinco [θíŋko], banco [báŋko], manco [máŋko], pongo and lengua with [ŋ], and monja, enjambre and fingir with [ŋ] before [x]. § 111 (p. 86) gives the velar nasal in cinco, and § 149 (p. 134) in nunca and lonja. On p. 112 the contact of the tongue with the velum «es completo cuando esta consonante va seguida de alguna de las oclusivas g, k; pero no suele serlo ante la fricativa x y mucho menos ante la semiconsonante w, llegando la ŋ con frecuencia en este último caso a reducirse a una simple nasalización de la vocal anterior». So the nasal is [ŋ] before k ɡ x w, the class that ES_EXT_FINAL_N_VELAR uses across words, and before ɣ where a child spirantizes /ɡ/. The nasal vowel that often replaces [ŋ] before w is not encoded. The rule takes only a coda nasal. In anual [aˈnwal] and continuo [konˈtinwo] the nasal begins the syllable of the glide, so it is not syllable-final and stays [n].

Fricative /b/ after any segment but a nasal. Navarro Tomás 1918, § 82 p. 63: «Se pronuncia, pues, fricativa toda b que no se halle en posición inicial absoluta ni precedida de m o n», with alba, arboleda, estorbo (p. 63) and esbelto, albañil (p. 64). The rule covers ⟨v⟩, which is the same /b/. A word-initial /b/ has no preceding segment in its word, so it keeps the stop here; ES_EXT_SPIRANT_B decides it from the preceding word.

Fricative /d/ after any segment but a nasal or /l/. Navarro Tomás 1918, § 101 p. 75: the stop occurs «cuando va en posición inicial absoluta o en contacto con una n o l precedentes. … En todo otro caso la d ortográfica toma el sonido đ», restated in § 102 p. 76. Examples: madre, piedra, cuadro, perdón (p. 77); the stop stays in falda, toldo, conde, mundo (p. 75).

Fricative /ɡ/ after any segment but a nasal. Navarro Tomás 1918, § 128 p. 108: the stop appears in absolute initial position and «en contacto con una nasal precedente»; § 129 p. 109: «Resulta, pues, normalmente fricativa toda g ortográfica … que en la pronunciación no se halle inicial absoluta ni precedida de n», with cargo, colgar, rasguño, siglo, alegre, digno. The segment rule also reaches the /ɡ/ of ⟨gu ante a o⟩ and ⟨güe güi⟩.

sandhi_rules.name: initial b after a non-nasal word end
sandhi_rules.notes: Phrase-level spirantization: the rule of § 82, § 101 and § 129 is stated on the phrase, not the word, so a word-initial stop after a word that ends in another segment is fricative. Navarro Tomás 1918 gives the cross-word cases himself: la boca, su boda, la brocha (§ 82 p. 63), el bollo, las bocas, por bailar (§ 83 p. 64); tu dinero, lo dicho, dos docenas (§ 102 pp. 76-77). The stop stays after a nasal (un día, un grado) and, for /d/, after /l/ (el domingo, § 101 p. 75). A pause between the words blocks the rule.

sandhi_rules.name: initial d after a word end other than a nasal or l
sandhi_rules.notes: Phrase-level spirantization: the rule of § 82, § 101 and § 129 is stated on the phrase, not the word, so a word-initial stop after a word that ends in another segment is fricative. Navarro Tomás 1918 gives the cross-word cases himself: la boca, su boda, la brocha (§ 82 p. 63), el bollo, las bocas, por bailar (§ 83 p. 64); tu dinero, lo dicho, dos docenas (§ 102 pp. 76-77). The stop stays after a nasal (un día, un grado) and, for /d/, after /l/ (el domingo, § 101 p. 75). A pause between the words blocks the rule.

sandhi_rules.name: initial g after a non-nasal word end
sandhi_rules.notes: Phrase-level spirantization: the rule of § 82, § 101 and § 129 is stated on the phrase, not the word, so a word-initial stop after a word that ends in another segment is fricative. Navarro Tomás 1918 gives the cross-word cases himself: la boca, su boda, la brocha (§ 82 p. 63), el bollo, las bocas, por bailar (§ 83 p. 64); tu dinero, lo dicho, dos docenas (§ 102 pp. 76-77). The stop stays after a nasal (un día, un grado) and, for /d/, after /l/ (el domingo, § 101 p. 75). A pause between the words blocks the rule.

sandhi_rules.name: word-final nasal before a labial
sandhi_rules.notes: A word-final nasal takes the place of the first consonant of the next word. Navarro Tomás (1918, § 87, p. 66): «En contacto con estas mismas consonantes iniciales de palabra, la n final de una palabra anterior se pronuncia también m», un buen baile [um bwem baile], en pie [em pjé]. So it is [m] before p b β m, the set of ES_NASAL_LABIAL inside a word. Navarro Tomás (1918, § 133, pp. 111-112): «La n final de sílaba, en contacto con una consonante velar siguiente, se asimila en la conversación ordinaria, por lo que a la posición de la lengua se refiere, a la articulación de dicha consonante velar», en casa [eŋ kása], sin gana [siŋ gána]. Before w the [ŋ] «con frecuencia» reduces to a nasal vowel (p. 112): un huerto [ũ wérto], con huevo [kõ wébo]. So it is [ŋ] before k ɡ x w. Where word-final /n/ is the velar [ŋ] (Lipski 2011, p. 7), the [ŋ] stays only before a pause, a vowel, a glide or a velar: Lipski (1986, p. 140) writes the rule as n → ŋ / __ # [−cons], and pp. 146-147: «the velarization of word-final preconsonantal /n/ is relatively less common in most dialects (Zamora and Guitart 1982:116), and the velarization of word-internal preconsonantal /n/ is rarer still. This is due to the normal process of homorganic assimilation of nasal consonants to following obstruents». Before a coronal or palatal consonant the nasal is [n], the value es-ES gives a nasal before such a consonant inside a word (enfermo [enˈfeɾmo], ancho [ˈantʃo]).

sandhi_rules.name: word-final nasal before a coronal or palatal consonant
sandhi_rules.notes: A word-final nasal takes the place of the first consonant of the next word. Navarro Tomás (1918, § 87, p. 66): «En contacto con estas mismas consonantes iniciales de palabra, la n final de una palabra anterior se pronuncia también m», un buen baile [um bwem baile], en pie [em pjé]. So it is [m] before p b β m, the set of ES_NASAL_LABIAL inside a word. Navarro Tomás (1918, § 133, pp. 111-112): «La n final de sílaba, en contacto con una consonante velar siguiente, se asimila en la conversación ordinaria, por lo que a la posición de la lengua se refiere, a la articulación de dicha consonante velar», en casa [eŋ kása], sin gana [siŋ gána]. Before w the [ŋ] «con frecuencia» reduces to a nasal vowel (p. 112): un huerto [ũ wérto], con huevo [kõ wébo]. So it is [ŋ] before k ɡ x w. Where word-final /n/ is the velar [ŋ] (Lipski 2011, p. 7), the [ŋ] stays only before a pause, a vowel, a glide or a velar: Lipski (1986, p. 140) writes the rule as n → ŋ / __ # [−cons], and pp. 146-147: «the velarization of word-final preconsonantal /n/ is relatively less common in most dialects (Zamora and Guitart 1982:116), and the velarization of word-internal preconsonantal /n/ is rarer still. This is due to the normal process of homorganic assimilation of nasal consonants to following obstruents». Before a coronal or palatal consonant the nasal is [n], the value es-ES gives a nasal before such a consonant inside a word (enfermo [enˈfeɾmo], ancho [ˈantʃo]).

sandhi_rules.name: word-final nasal before a velar or w
sandhi_rules.notes: A word-final nasal takes the place of the first consonant of the next word. Navarro Tomás (1918, § 87, p. 66): «En contacto con estas mismas consonantes iniciales de palabra, la n final de una palabra anterior se pronuncia también m», un buen baile [um bwem baile], en pie [em pjé]. So it is [m] before p b β m, the set of ES_NASAL_LABIAL inside a word. Navarro Tomás (1918, § 133, pp. 111-112): «La n final de sílaba, en contacto con una consonante velar siguiente, se asimila en la conversación ordinaria, por lo que a la posición de la lengua se refiere, a la articulación de dicha consonante velar», en casa [eŋ kása], sin gana [siŋ gána]. Before w the [ŋ] «con frecuencia» reduces to a nasal vowel (p. 112): un huerto [ũ wérto], con huevo [kõ wébo]. So it is [ŋ] before k ɡ x w. Where word-final /n/ is the velar [ŋ] (Lipski 2011, p. 7), the [ŋ] stays only before a pause, a vowel, a glide or a velar: Lipski (1986, p. 140) writes the rule as n → ŋ / __ # [−cons], and pp. 146-147: «the velarization of word-final preconsonantal /n/ is relatively less common in most dialects (Zamora and Guitart 1982:116), and the velarization of word-internal preconsonantal /n/ is rarer still. This is due to the normal process of homorganic assimilation of nasal consonants to following obstruents». Before a coronal or palatal consonant the nasal is [n], the value es-ES gives a nasal before such a consonant inside a word (enfermo [enˈfeɾmo], ancho [ˈantʃo]).
